name: Sardinian cantu a tenore
lineage: Sardinian cantu a tenore four-male-voice polyphonic tradition of the Barbagia region (interior central-northeast Sardinia, particularly the Nuoro province villages of Bitti, Orgosolo, Orune, and Orosei). The ensemble consists of four named voice-parts: the boghe (the soloist who initiates each verse with the verse-text, leading the ensemble), the mesu boghe (the high tenor-register harmony voice), the contra (the guttural-ventricular harmony voice producing a deep bass-register growl through false-vocal-fold co-oscillation), and the bassu (the lowest guttural-ventricular voice, producing the deepest growling subharmonic). The contra and bassu employ the same false-vocal-fold technique that produces Tuvan kargyraa subharmonic — a striking case of independent convergence between two unrelated traditions. Performance occurs traditionally in the su zilleri stone-walled village bar, with the four singers facing inward in a tight circle. Repertoire spans religious processional cycles (such as the Holy Week passion-passages), pastoral courtship and praise songs, and the satirical-improvisatory cantu a tenore-with-improvised-text contest contexts. Tenores di Bitti and Tenores di Orosei among the canonical twentieth-century ensembles. Bernard Lortat-Jacob's Chants de Passion (Éditions du Cerf 1998) and the Smithsonian Folkways SFW 50402 Sardinia: Music of the Shepherds (1995) constitute the principal documentary anchors. Distinguished from Corsican paghjella by Sardinian's four-voice (vs Corsican three-voice) configuration and guttural-ventricular subharmonic vocal architecture; distinguished from Albanian iso-polyphony by Sardinian's no-drone subharmonic-voice-as-bass (vs Albanian iso-drone foundation) configuration.
